subtitle: An Excel root cause analysis that tested every explanation for a sudden checkout drop until one was left, and costed it.
seo_description: Business analysis case study: Excel root cause analysis of an e-commerce checkout conversion drop using data-quality checks, two-proportion z-tests, segment analysis and a revenue impact bridge.

sections.title: Executive summary
paragraphs: Checkout completion fell sharply in June 2026 and revenue fell with it. The product team suspected an ongoing **PayPal integration issue**. I built a single Excel workbook that answers four questions in order: is the data clean enough to trust, when did the decline start, which segments cause it, and how much revenue it has cost.

**The answer: PayQuick, a new payment option, is the cause. PayPal is not.** PayQuick went live at 00:03 on 18 June, the same minute the decline began, and 95% of PayQuick checkouts time out at order authorisation.
sections.callout: The dataset is a **practice case dataset** of a fictional online store. Every figure in the workbook is a live formula, cross-checked by a separate Python analysis.

sections.title: Business problem
paragraphs: A drop in checkout completion is expensive every day it continues, and fixing the wrong cause wastes engineering time. The business needed a defensible root cause, a cost estimate and a plan, quickly.

sections.title: Analytical objectives
list: Confirm the data is trustworthy before analysing it.
Find the break date statistically rather than by eye.
Test every plausible hypothesis (PayPal, device or browser, traffic mix, a coupon campaign, the new payment option) and rule each in or out.
Estimate the revenue lost, and the cost of every further day without a fix.

sections.title: Dataset
paragraphs: 26,375 checkout sessions from June 2026, with payment method, device, OS, browser, region, traffic source, coupon, checkout stage reached, error codes and order value.

sections.title: Data cleaning & validation
paragraphs: The **1_Cleaning** sheet runs 13 live data-quality checks before any analysis: duplicates, blanks, invalid values, contradictions between fields and outliers. The cleaned sessions sit in an Excel table that every other sheet reads from.

sections.title: Analytical methodology
list: **Break date:** daily metrics plus a scan of every possible break date using a **two-proportion z-test**; the date is selected by formula (`INDEX`/`MATCH` on the z-score scan).
**Segments:** before-versus-after completion for 30 segments with z-tests, the result with PayQuick removed, and where each payment method's sessions stop in checkout.
**Revenue impact:** three independent methods (session-level estimate, top-down and outlier-capped) plus a revenue bridge.
**Cross-check:** `tollgate_rca.py` repeats the whole analysis in Python; every Excel number matches.

kpis: Completed orders ÷ sessions that reached checkout

sections.title: The workbook
paragraphs: Seven sheets: Dashboard, Executive Summary, 1_Cleaning, 2_Break_Date, 3_Segments, 4_Revenue and Data. Chart titles state their conclusion, and summary sentences are built with `TEXT()` so they update with the data.

sections.title: Key findings
findings: **The decline began at 00:03 on 18 June,** the minute PayQuick went live.
**95% of PayQuick checkouts time out** at order authorisation (`PAYMENT_AUTH_TIMEOUT`), and every timeout is a PayQuick session.
**Completion fell from 68.7% to 59.1%.** With PayQuick sessions excluded it is 68.8%, unchanged.
**PayPal was ruled out:** 69.6% → 68.8%, not significant (p = 0.45), with zero timeouts.
**Estimated loss: $70,943 in 13 days,** about $164K every 30 days if unfixed.

sections.title: Recommendations
list: Hide PayQuick at checkout today.
Fix the authorisation timeout with the vendor.
Relaunch to 5% of traffic first, with alerts on completion by payment method.
Email the 1,595 customers it turned away ($104K in carts).

sections.title: Technical implementation
list: `COUNTIFS` and `SUMIFS` for every metric, driven by a single break-date cell.
Two-proportion z-tests with `SQRT` and `NORMSDIST`; `SUMPRODUCT` for consistency checks and the outlier-capped estimate.
`MINIFS`, `MAXIFS`, `PERCENTILE` and `QUARTILE` for outlier detection.
Native charts, including a waterfall built from stacked columns; a colour convention for inputs, links and formulas.
Python (pandas, NumPy, openpyxl) to clean the data, cross-check the analysis and build the workbook.

sections.title: Limitations & assumptions
list: The data is a practice case, not a real store's sessions.
Revenue loss is an estimate; three methods are shown so the range is visible.
Statistical tests show association in observational data; the timing, error codes and removal test together make the causal case.
